lessons.title: આંખ (āṅkh) — an eye, and a nasal that is not what it looks like
lessons.gloss: eye — a straight cousin of the English word, and a nasal mark that is not the neuter tell you might expect

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page

segments.text: બહેન (bahen) closed a chapter about people. This chapter checks on how someone is — starting with the parts of the body a friend might actually ask about.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word

segments.text: આંખ — āṅkh — eye.

આ the independent long-ā, then the nasal dot ં sitting on top of it — exactly the medial anusvāra you first read inside વાંચવું, doing the same job here, in the middle of a noun rather than a verb — then ખ, the aspirated k. Note what this nasal is NOT: it does not mark આંખ (āṅkh) as neuter — the word is feminine. A nasal dot in the middle of a word is a sound, present or absent as pronunciation happens to need it; it is a different thing entirely from the grammatical -ũ ending you will meet again soon, and this chapter keeps the two apart on purpose.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the same word as "eye," unbroken

segments.text: āṅkh is inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit akkhi, from Sanskrit akṣi, "eye." The root is Indo-European h₃ekʷ-, "eye; to see," and it survives unbroken in English eye itself, in Latin oculus (behind ocular), and in Greek ósse. This is bhāī's kind of cousin, not bahen's: a straight line back to the same ancestor, no borrowing and no detour.

lessons.title: કાન (kān) — an ear whose own root is unsettled
lessons.gloss: ear — a word Sanskrit itself could not settle the origin of, and one that changed gender on the way to Gujarati

segments.text: આંખ (āṅkh) traced back cleanly to a confirmed Indo-European root. The next body part will not be nearly as tidy.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word

segments.text: કાન — kān — ear.
ક ka, ા long-ā, ન na. All three already yours.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: a gender that changed on the way here

segments.text: કાન is feminine in Gujarati. Its Sanskrit ancestor, karṇa, was masculine. Nothing about inheriting a word guarantees its gender comes along unchanged — મિત્ર kept Sanskrit's masculine, but kān did not keep karṇa's. Gender, like the gender of આંખ (āṅkh) or બહેન, has to be learned with each noun as it stands today, not projected backward from what its ancestor was — the same caution રોટલી's chapter drew from its own -ī ending.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — where even Sanskrit scholars disagree

segments.text: kān is inherited from Old Gujarati kāna, through Apabhramsa and Prakrit kaṇṇa, from Sanskrit karṇa, "ear." Past that point, no agreement exists. Proposed origins include a root for "defect" (with "ear" as a later, narrower sense), a root meaning "point" or "spike," a root meaning "handle" or "grip," and a connection to śṛṇoti, "to hear." None of these has won out. Kān joins roṭlī as a second word in your Gujarati vocabulary whose Sanskrit form is certain and whose deeper root is not — the honest answer, said plainly rather than picked at random.

lessons.title: મોઢું (moḍhũ) — the tell you have been hearing all along
lessons.gloss: mouth — the clearest example yet of Gujarati's neuter tell, the nasalized -ũ you have been hearing on every verb

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: કાન (kān)'s own gender shifted away from Sanskrit's. The next body part wears its gender in plain sight — the same nasalized ending you have heard on nearly every verb in this book.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word

segments.text: મોઢું — moḍhũ — mouth.
મ ma, ો the o sign, then a new letter: ઢ, the retroflex aspirated ḍh — curl the tongue back as for ટ and ણ, and add the puff of breath that made ધ aspirated. Then ું, u with the nasal dot. Mo-ḍhũ.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the neuter tell, named plainly

segments.text: Every verb infinitive in this book ends in the neuter -વું: hovũ, javũ, jāṇvũ, lakhvũ — a whole word class marked by that one nasalized ending. મોઢું shows the same ending doing the same job on a noun: moḍhũ is neuter, and the nasalized -ũ is the single most recognizable tell for it. Not every neuter noun wears it — પાણી and નાક (nāk) do not — but when you do see or hear a word end this way, neuter is the way to bet. And do not confuse it with આંખ (āṅkh)'s nasal: that one sat in the middle of a feminine word and marked nothing about gender at all. This one sits at the end, and it does.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — a mouth, and a doublet with its own formal twin

segments.text: moḍhũ is inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit muha, from Sanskrit mukha, "mouth, face." It has a formal doublet, મુખ mukh, borrowed directly from the same Sanskrit word the way kuṭumb was — the everyday and the formal register, side by side, from one ancestor reached by two different roads. Past Sanskrit, mukha's own root is not agreed upon — a second open question, alongside karṇa's, rather than a guess dressed up as an answer.

lessons.title: નાક (nāk) — the whole face, run back
lessons.gloss: nose — the fourth body word, closing the chapter by running the whole face back through gender, sound, and certainty

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page

segments.text: આંખ (āṅkh), કાન (kān), મોઢું (moḍhũ) — eye, ear, mouth. One more completes the face, and this one closes the chapter by tying its ending back to a pattern from three chapters ago.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word

segments.text: નાક — nāk — nose.
ન na, ા long-ā, ક ka. Every letter already familiar — nāk's only new information is the word itself.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: closing the chapter's gender count

segments.text: નાક is neuter, like મોઢું — but unlike moḍhũ, it carries no nasalized -ũ at all. Run the whole face: āṅkh feminine, kān feminine, moḍhũ neuter with the tell, nāk neuter without it. Two neuters, only one of them wearing the ending that names the class. This is exactly why last lesson called the nasalized -ũ a tell, not a rule: it is the loudest signal Gujarati gives you for neuter, and it is still only sometimes there — the same caution roṭlī and pāṇī already taught you about -ī, and kān's Grammar Lens taught you about gender and inheritance more generally.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the last unbroken cousin in the chapter

segments.text: nāk is inherited from Prakrit ṇakka, from Sanskrit nas, "nose," with a suffix added along the way — the retroflex ṇ here is the same sound-shift you first met turning jānāti into jāṇvũ, a single letter's worth of difference deciding a great deal, the way one mark once told javũ apart from jovũ. The root is Indo-European nehas-, unbroken in English nose, Latin nāsus (behind nasal), and Lithuanian nósis. Like āṅkh, nāk needed no ship and no loan to reach you — only the ordinary work of sound change, the same work that once put a nasal dot in the middle of વાંચવું and, this chapter, in the middle of આંખ.
